title: Tenali Raman Tale 88
summary: Envious courtiers who wanted to eliminate Tenali Raman convinced King Krishnadevaraya that royal health required an extraordinary medicin...
full_text:
Envious courtiers who wanted to eliminate Tenali Raman convinced King Krishnadevaraya that royal health required an extraordinary medicine:
'Maharaj, your royal vitality requires the most potent tonic known to Ayurveda: pure, fresh milk from a wild tigress nursing her cubs in the jungle!
Only a man of supreme courage and resourcefulness can fetch it—and none is more capable than Tenali Raman!'

The King, in a whimsical mood, commanded Tenali:
'Tenali, venture into the Dandaka forest and bring me a cup of fresh tigress's milk within seven days, or face royal displeasure!'

The courtiers smirked, expecting Tenali to be torn to pieces by tigers or banished for failure.
Tenali bowed: 'Your command shall be fulfilled, Maharaj.'

Tenali did not walk into the tiger’s lair to be eaten.
He went to the village of a pastoral shepherd community and found a magnificent, large wild mountain goat whose milk was unusually thick and creamy.
Tenali paid the shepherd for a brass pot of the rich goat's milk.

Tenali then spent five days walking through thorny mountain brush, deliberately tearing his silk coat, scratching his arms and face with harmless brambles, and rubbing red clay onto his trousers.

On the seventh day, Tenali staggered into King Krishnadevaraya’s audience hall.
He looked battered, bleeding from minor scratches, his clothes in rags, panting as though he had wrestled ten demons!
In his trembling hand, he held a sealed golden goblet covered with a tiger skin!

The King sprang from his throne in alarm:
'Tenali! What happened to thee? Thou art wounded!'

Tenali gasped with theatrical heroism:
'Jahanpanah! I fought through the deepest caves of the Dandaka jungle!
I located a fierce, ten-foot man-eating tigress nursing four cubs!
I wrestled the beast for three hours, pinned her claws to the cave wall, and milked this cup from her breast with my own hands!
Here is your tigress’s milk, Maharaj!'

The King stared at the goblet, then at the blood and torn clothes on Tenali:
'Tenali, this is miraculous valor!'

Tenali smiled and said:
'However, Maharaj, the royal physicians who prescribed this medicine must administer it!
Our ancient Ayurvedic texts state that whoever drinks tigress's milk must also be massaged with the tigress’s claws, and the courtiers who suggested this cure must accompany me back to the jungle to return the tigress her cup!'

The envious courtiers turned green with absolute terror, falling to their knees, begging the King:
'No, no, Your Majesty! The cure is too dangerous! We withdraw the recommendation!'

The King laughed, realizing the brilliant comedy of Tenali’s adventure.
He rewarded Tenali with five hundred gold coins for his 'heroic scratches', while the schemers learned never to set traps for the master of wit.
moral: When power demands impossible and perilous tasks, wit provides a safe and humorous escape.
